formulations.label: Film-coated tablets
formulations.note: 10 mg tablets are for 15 years and over. Contains lactose. Other UK forms (5 mg and 4 mg chewable tablets, 4 mg granules) are for younger children and were not reviewed here.

src.q: One film-coated tablet contains montelukast sodium, which is equivalent to 10 mg montelukast.
Do not give Singulair 10 mg film-coated tablets to children less than 15 years of age.
This medicine contains 89.3 mg lactose monohydrate per tablet.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Add-on treatment of mild to moderate persistent asthma not controlled by inhaled corticosteroids plus as-needed short-acting beta-agonist; in these patients it can also relieve seasonal allergic rhinitis. Prevention of asthma where exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is the main component.

src.q: indicated in the treatment of asthma as add-on therapy in those patients with mild to moderate persistent asthma who are inadequately controlled on inhaled corticosteroids
Singulair can also provide symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis
Singulair is also indicated in the prophylaxis of asthma in which the predominant component is exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

items.t: Not for treating an acute asthma attack. Do not use with other montelukast-containing products. Do not substitute abruptly for inhaled or oral corticosteroids.

src.q: Patients should be advised never to use oral montelukast to treat acute asthma attacks
Singulair should not be used concomitantly with other products containing the same active ingredient, montelukast.
Montelukast should not be substituted abruptly for inhaled or oral corticosteroids.

items.t: 10 mg once daily in the evening.
items.tag: Asthma (with or without seasonal allergic rhinitis), adults and adolescents 15 years and over

src.q: is one 10 mg tablet daily to be taken in the evening

items.t: Do not give the 10 mg tablet under 15 years; safety and efficacy not established. Other forms exist: 5 mg chewable tablets (6-14 years), 4 mg chewable tablets (2-5 years), 4 mg granules (6 months-5 years).

src.q: Do not give Singulair 10 mg film-coated tablets to children less than 15 years of age.

5 mg chewable tablets are available for paediatric patients 6 to 14 years of age. 4 mg chewable tablets are available for paediatric patients 2 to 5 years of age. 4 mg granules are available for paediatric patients 6 months to 5 years of age.

items.t: MHRA: in children, nightmares, aggression and anxiety are the most reported neuropsychiatric reactions; in teenagers, anxiety, suicidal ideation and depression.

src.q: The most frequently reported reactions in younger children (up to and including 12 years old) were aggression, nightmares and anxiety
in older children (13 years old up to and including 17 years old) the most commonly reported were anxiety, suicidal ideation and depression

items.t: Hypersensitivity to montelukast or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Neuropsychiatric reactions (sleep disorders, nightmares, depression, agitation, aggression, hallucinations, suicidal thoughts and behaviour) occur in all age groups and may be serious. MHRA (2024) and one UK SmPC: stop montelukast if new or worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms occur. Another UK SmPC: carefully weigh the risks and benefits of continuing.

src.q: discontinue montelukast if patients experience new or worsening symptoms of neuropsychiatric reactions
Therefore, the treatment with montelukast should be discontinued if neuropsychiatric symptoms occur during treatment.
Prescribers should carefully evaluate the risks and benefits of continuing treatment with Singulair if such events occur.

items.t: Eosinophilia, sometimes with vasculitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), rarely occurs, sometimes when oral steroids are reduced. Watch for eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worse lung symptoms, heart complications or neuropathy; reassess treatment.

src.q: physicians should be alert to eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worsening pulmonary symptoms, cardiac complications, and/or neuropathy presenting in their patients
Patients who develop these symptoms should be reassessed and their treatment regimens evaluated.

items.t: Aspirin-sensitive asthma: montelukast does not remove the need to avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs.

src.q: Treatment with montelukast does not alter the need for patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma to avoid taking aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, the Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Inducers of CYP3A4, 2C8 and 2C9 (for example phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin) lower montelukast levels; use with caution, especially in children.

src.q: caution should be exercised, particularly in children, when montelukast is co-administered with inducers of CYP 3A4, 2C8, and 2C9, such as phenytoin, phenobarbital and rifampicin

items.t: Gemfibrozil (strong CYP2C8 and 2C9 inhibitor) raised montelukast exposure 4.4-fold: no routine dose change, but be aware of more adverse effects. Itraconazole (strong CYP3A4 inhibitor) did not raise exposure significantly.

src.q: gemfibrozil increased the systemic exposure of montelukast by 4.4-fold
Co-administration of montelukast with itraconazole, a strong inhibitor of CYP 3A4, resulted in no significant increase in the systemic exposure of montelukast.

items.t: No clinically important effect on theophylline, prednisolone, oral contraceptives, digoxin or warfarin. Not expected to change the metabolism of CYP2C8 substrates such as repaglinide.

src.q: theophylline, prednisone, prednisolone, oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone 35/1), terfenadine, digoxin and warfarin
montelukast is not anticipated to markedly alter the metabolism of medicinal products metabolised by this enzyme (e.g., paclitaxel, rosiglitazone, and repaglinide)

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal insufficiency.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary for the elderly, or for patients with renal insufficiency, or mild to moderate hepatic impairment.

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: no dose adjustment. Severe hepatic impairment: no data.

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary for the elderly, or for patients with renal insufficiency, or mild to moderate hepatic impairment.
There are no data on patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: SmPC: published data have not shown a drug-related risk of major birth defects (studies have limitations); use in pregnancy only if clearly essential.

src.q: Available data from published prospective and retrospective cohort studies with montelukast use in pregnant women evaluating major birth defects have not established a drug-associated risk.
Singulair may be used during pregnancy only if it is considered to be clearly essential.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor; available information does not raise concern for the baby.

src.q: Montelukast can be used during pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
The available information does not raise concern that use of montelukast in pregnancy causes problems for your baby.

items.t: SPS (hay fever in pregnancy): due to lack of information, do not use montelukast only for allergic rhinitis; it may be used for co-existing asthma.

src.q: montelukast should not be used solely to treat allergic rhinitis, but may be used to treat concomitant asthma

items.t: Excreted in rat milk; unknown in human milk. Use in breastfeeding only if clearly essential.

src.q: It is unknown whether montelukast/metabolites are excreted in human milk.
Singulair may be used in breast-feeding only if it is considered to be clearly essential.

items.t: BUMPS: no increased risk to the baby expected if the father takes montelukast.

src.q: We do not expect any increased risk to your baby if the father takes montelukast.

items.t: Very common: upper respiratory infection. Common: headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, rash, fever, raised ALT/AST.

src.q: upper respiratory infection† Very Common
diarrhoea‡, nausea‡, vomiting‡ Common
elevated levels of serum transaminases (ALT, AST) Common

items.t: Neuropsychiatric reactions: depression, agitation and aggression, sleep disturbance (up to 1 in 100); attention or memory problems; very rarely hallucinations and suicidal thinking and behaviour. Stop montelukast if new or worsening symptoms (MHRA 2024).

src.q: very rarely, hallucinations and suicidal thinking and behaviour (up to 1 in 10,000 people)
discontinue montelukast if patients experience new or worsening symptoms of neuropsychiatric reactions

items.t: Churg-Strauss syndrome, pulmonary eosinophilia, hepatitis, anaphylaxis, erythema multiforme (rare or very rare).

src.q: Churg-Strauss Syndrome (CSS) (see section 4.4) Very Rare
hepatitis (including cholestatic, hepatocellular, and mixed-pattern liver injury). Very Rare
hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis Uncommon

items.t: Be alert for neuropsychiatric reactions in all patients, including children and adolescents.

src.q: be alert for neuropsychiatric reactions in patients taking montelukast; events have been reported in adults, adolescents, and children

items.t: Stop if new or worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms (MHRA 2024; one UK SmPC). Reassess if signs of eosinophilic vasculitis.

src.q: discontinue montelukast if patients experience new or worsening symptoms of neuropsychiatric reactions
Patients who develop these symptoms should be reassessed and their treatment regimens evaluated.

items.t: Once daily in the evening, with or without food.

src.q: is one 10 mg tablet daily to be taken in the evening
Singulair may be taken with or without food.

items.t: Keep taking it even when asthma is controlled and during flare-ups. Keep a reliever inhaler for attacks; see a doctor if the reliever is needed more than usual.

src.q: Patients should be advised to continue taking Singulair even if their asthma is under control, as well as during periods of worsening asthma.
Patients should seek their doctors' advice as soon as possible if they need more inhalations of short-acting β-agonists than usual.

items.t: Mood, sleep or behaviour changes (nightmares, aggression, anxiety, thoughts of self-harm) can occur: seek medical attention at once. Tell family and friends you take montelukast, as they may notice changes first.

src.q: you should seek immediate medical attention if you or your child experiences these symptoms
it is very important to tell your friends and family that you are taking montelukast
